# Results — Study 266 (Misery-Index) on the S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). December CPI-YoY and
unemployment are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../misery_index/data.py) (1948–2025);
S&P 500 calendar-year price returns are December/December closes from the
repo-level cache `_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`. Match the fingerprint below
to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 (Yahoo ^GSPC, nominal price, December/December) | returns 1950–2025 | 76 forward-return years | `1330e38af625` |
| Misery table (CPI-U Dec YoY + Dec U-3 unemployment) | 1948–2025 | hardcoded constant | — |

The misery print of December year *Y* is matched to the S&P return of year
*Y+1* (one full-year execution lag, no look-ahead). The merged panel runs over
misery-years 1949–2024 → return-years 1950–2025 (n = 76).

## The unconditional base rate — the key number

The S&P 500 rose in **73.7%** of the 76 forward-return years. This is the
correct null for any "buy when misery is high" rule: a contrarian timing signal
that says "be long" inherits this up-rate for free, so the question is whether
high-misery years *beat* 73.7%, not 50%.

## Predictive regressions (forward annual return on standardized predictor)

Slopes are per 1-SD of the predictor; the headline statistic is the Newey-West
(HAC, 3-lag) t-stat.

| Predictor | β per 1-SD | OLS t | **HAC t** | R² |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Misery **level** (Dec) | **+0.09 pp** | +0.045 | **+0.075** | 0.000 |
| Misery **change** (YoY) | −0.40 pp | −0.210 | **−0.231** | 0.001 |

Both slopes are economically and statistically null. A 1-SD swing in the misery
index (≈ 3.5 points of inflation+unemployment) moves the predicted next-year
return by less than a tenth of a percentage point, with a HAC t-stat under 0.1.
Neither the leading-bear (negative slope) nor the contrarian (positive slope)
story is supported.

## High-minus-low tercile sort (the contrarian "buy the bottom" test)

| Tercile | n | mean forward return | up-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Low misery (calm economy) | 26 | **+9.2%** | 66.7% |
| Mid misery | 24 | +10.7% | — |
| High misery (max pessimism) | 26 | **+9.0%** | 77.8% |

- **High-minus-low spread: −0.2 pp** — the contrarian "buy when misery is high"
  bet does *not* out-return the calm-economy years. Welch t = **−0.06**,
  p = **0.95**. The high-misery up-rate (77.8%) is only +4.1pp above the 73.7%
  base rate — pure sampling noise on 26 observations.

## Sub-period stability

| Window | n | misery-level β | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1950–1987 (return-year) | 38 | +0.73 pp | +0.46 |
| 1988–2025 (return-year) | 38 | −0.62 pp | −0.29 |

The slope *flips sign* across halves — the hallmark of a non-effect. Whatever
mild positive tilt the stagflation era contributes is reversed in the modern
sample.

## The n = 76 power problem

With 76 annual observations and ~17% annual S&P volatility, the minimum
detectable per-1-SD slope at 80% power (two-sided, α = 0.05) is:

    MDE ≈ (t_crit + t_power) · σ / √n ≈ 5.5 pp/yr per 1-SD.

The observed level slope is +0.09 pp — less than **2%** of the detectable
threshold. Even before accounting for the serial correlation of macro regimes
(which shrinks the *effective* n further), the sample cannot resolve an effect
of any plausible size.

## Could you trade it?

The contrarian timing rule — long the S&P only in the year after a top-tercile
(high-misery) December print, flat otherwise:

| Strategy | Annualized CAGR (price-only) |
|---|--:|
| Buy & hold S&P | **+8.2%** |
| Misery-timing, gross | +2.7% |
| Misery-timing, **net** (10 bps one-way × NAV) | **+2.7%** |

- The rule sits in the market only **35.5%** of years (frac in-market 0.355),
  forfeiting the equity premium in the other ~64%.
- Turnover is low (**0.16 switches/yr**), so costs are negligible — gross ≈ net.
  The shortfall is **−5.5 pp/yr** vs buy-and-hold and is entirely an
  opportunity-cost story, not a transaction-cost one.

Returns are **price-only** (no dividends), which understates buy-and-hold's true
edge; on a total-return basis the timing rule loses by even more.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Misery-level HAC t = +0.08, misery-change HAC t = −0.23,
  tercile spread −0.2 pp (Welch t = −0.06, p = 0.95), and the slope flips sign
  across sub-periods. No version of the misery index carries forward content for
  next-year S&P returns. The S&P is the index itself (survivorship-clean), so
  this null is not an artifact of basket selection.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The contrarian timing rule earns +2.7%/yr net vs
  +8.2%/yr buy-and-hold — it is dominated by simply staying invested.
- **Busted — a welfare gauge, not a market timer.** The misery index measures
  how bad the economy feels; it says nothing reliable about where stocks go next.
